newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechens upbeat, Russians cautious on independence.
newsitem.headline: Chechens upbeat, Russians cautious on independence.

text.p: Chechen leader Aslan Maskhadov said on Monday he was pleased after talks with Russian President Boris Yeltsin and said he had high hopes of negotiating formal independence for his breakaway republic.

But the chief Russian negotiator with Chechnya, Ivan Rybkin, poured cold water on Maskhadov's optimism and made clear that Moscow would not formally recognise the region's independence despite its readiness to grant Chechnya strong autonomy.
"We are pressing today for the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria to be recognised as an independent sovereign state," Maskhadov told a news conference. "In what form, time will tell."

"During this lengthy discussion between two presidents both came to the common opinion that we must take this step," he added, saying it was vital for stability not just in Chechnya but in Russia and ordinary Russians would support the move.

"Today I saw in the president of the Russian Federation a man, perhaps the only man, who can decide matters...and make peace after 400 years of war," he said. "Decisiveness is demanded, one must take responsibility, I think Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin) possesses such characteristics."

Maskhadov said he hoped a joint Chechen-Russian commission could begin work as early as next week on agreeing a final political settlement, an outline of which the Chechens had presented to Yeltsin on Monday.

He said he believed Yeltsin understood the Chechens' need for independence after their battle against Russia, which began under the tsars, and thought the Russian people were also prepared to recognise the region.

Russian news agencies earlier quoted Yeltsin as saying he was ready to negotiate a long-term political deal with Chechnya but made clear he still viewed the rebel region as an integral part of Russia.

Rybkin, who is also secretary of Yeltsin's policy-making Security Council, later hinted that Moscow was ready to consider most extravagant options for Chechnya as long as they did not look like an outright secession.

"There may be all sorts of statuses for the member of the Russian federation, there may be different sorts of enclaves and such," he told a separate news conference. "In any case I deeply believe that Russia's territorial integrity will not be harmed."
Rybkin also said Moscow had urged Maskhadov to take steps to free hundreds of Russians and several foreigners held hostage in Chechnya.
On Sunday Chechen commandos released two Russian reporters held hostage since mid-June.
Russian commercial NTV television said on Monday its three journalists held hostage for more than three month had been released earlier in the day.
The Chechens said the Russians were encouraging a wave of hostage-taking in and around Chechnya. Two Britons, a German, a Slovak and four French aid workers are still being held.
Maskhadov said the banditry was part of an "invisible war" against the Chechen nation that could only be ended if Russia granted it sovereignty.
